title: Where are you from?
goal: Say what country you come from and your nationality, ask about someone's job, and see how one small ending turns a country into a nationality.
bekal: ask and say where someone is from with *min aina* and *min*
build the nationality word for any country yourself
name jobs in both the male and the female form

dialogs.title: حِوَار — فِي الْمَقْهَى
dialogs.intro: At a coffee shop near the campus. Budi shares a table with a female student.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: أَهْلًا! أَنْتَ طَالِبٌ جَدِيدٌ، أَلَيْسَ كَذٰلِكَ؟
lines.baca: ahlan! anta ṭaalibun jadiid, alaisa kadhaalik?
lines.id: Hi! You're the new student, aren't you?
lines.literal: hi! you student new, isn't-it so?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Yes. I'm Budi. What's your name?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: My name is Laila. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا! أَنَا مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ. أَنَا مَغْرِبِيَّةٌ.
lines.baca: ahlan wa sahlan! anaa minal-maghrib. anaa maghribiyyah.
lines.id: Welcome! I'm from Morocco. I'm Moroccan.
lines.literal: welcome! I from the-Morocco. I Moroccan(f).

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: What do you do? Are you a student?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.baca: anaa ṭaalibatun wa mutarjimatun aiḍan. wa anta?
lines.id: I'm a student and also a translator. And you?
lines.literal: I student(f) and translator(f) also. and you?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I'm an engineer, and I'm studying Arabic here.
lines.literal: I engineer, and I-study the-Arabic here.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: No problem! This is just the beginning.

notes: **مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ — two question words joined.** أَيْنَ on its own means "where"; with مِنْ in front it becomes "where from". To a woman: مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟ The answer always uses مِنْ too: أَنَا مِنْ...

**Country vs nationality.** إِنْدُونِيسِيَا is the country; إِنْدُونِيسِيٌّ is the person. The only difference is the ending ـِيّ — and that is the one tool you need to form any nationality. The ending is called the **nisba**.
**Women add ة.** إِنْدُونِيسِيٌّ (male) → إِنْدُونِيسِيَّةٌ (female). Notice that لَيْلَى says مَغْرِبِيَّةٌ, not مَغْرِبِيٌّ — not out of politeness, but because grammar requires it.

**مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ, not مِنْ الْمَغْرِبِ.** The sukun on نْ turns into a fatha when it meets اَلْ, so that two vowelless letters don't collide: *minal-maghrib*, *minal-yaum*. The rule is automatic and there's no list to memorize — just follow the pronunciation line.

**Arab country names almost always take اَلْ.** اَلْمَغْرِب (Morocco), اَلْعِرَاق (Iraq), اَلْأُرْدُنّ (Jordan), اَلسُّودَان (Sudan), اَلْيَمَن (Yemen). Those that don't: مِصْر (Egypt), سُورِيَا (Syria), لُبْنَان (Lebanon), إِنْدُونِيسِيَا. There is no rule — this part you simply memorize.
**مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ literally "what is your work".** Notice that Arabic uses مَا (what) to ask about a job, not مَنْ (who). Another common option: مَاذَا تَعْمَلُ؟ ("what do you do?").
**لُغَتُكَ جَيِّدَةٌ — a nominal sentence again.** No "is". Notice too that جَيِّدَة is feminine because لُغَة (language) is a feminine word — the ة at the end decides that, not the meaning.

**لَا مُشْكِلَةَ** literally "there is no problem". This pattern — لَا + a noun without tanween — states an absolute "no ...": لَا بَأْسَ (no harm, it's fine), لَا شُكْرَ عَلَى وَاجِبٍ (no thanks needed for a duty).
**أَلَيْسَ كَذٰلِكَ؟** is the Arabic "isn't it?" — tagged onto the end of a sentence to ask for agreement, just like the English tag question.

grammars.title: The nisba — turning a place into a nationality
body: One ending, and the whole world map opens up. The method: drop a final ا or ة from the country name if there is one, then attach ـِيّ.
after: The nisba doesn't stop at countries. It works for anything: عَرَبِيّ (Arab, Arabic, from عَرَب), إِسْلَامِيّ (Islamic), يَوْمِيّ (daily, from يَوْم), جَامِعِيّ (university-, from جَامِعَة).

Language names are the feminine nisba: اَلْعَرَبِيَّة (Arabic), اَلْإِنْجِلِيزِيَّة (English), اَلْإِنْدُونِيسِيَّة (Indonesian). The full form is اَللُّغَةُ الْعَرَبِيَّةُ ("the Arabic language"), but the word لُغَة is almost always dropped.

grammars.title: Jobs — and their female counterparts
body: Almost every job title is masculine, and the feminine form simply adds ة.
after: Notice the مُ- at the front of many words: مُدَرِّس, مُهَنْدِس, مُتَرْجِم, مُمَرِّض. The prefix مُ almost always marks the **doer** — the person who does the job, much like English *-er*. Once you see the pattern, you can guess the meaning of new words built the same way.

blocks.text: City names work in exactly the same sentence: أَنَا مِنْ جَاكَرْتَا (I'm from Jakarta), أَنَا مِنْ بَانْدُونْج (I'm from Bandung), هُوَ مِنَ الْقَاهِرَةِ (he's from Cairo).

blocks.title: Why مِصْرَ has no tanween
items: In the unit 1 dialogue you saw مِنْ مِصْرَ, not مِنْ مِصْرٍ. Some proper names — especially place names and women's names — belong to a group that **refuses tanween**: مِصْر, مَكَّة, فَاطِمَة, أَحْمَد.
At A1 you don't need to memorize the list. One habit is enough: **proper names rarely take tanween.** This book always writes their final vowels correctly, so you can absorb it by eye.

blocks.text: Everything you learned for "you" works exactly the same for "he/she" — just swap the ending.

One important difference from English: مَا is used for **things**, مَنْ for **people**. Asking a name uses مَا, not مَنْ — مَا اسْمُكَ is literally "what is your name", because you're asking about the name, not the person. Here English happens to agree.

blocks.title: A ten-minute drill that works
items: Pick ten people you know. For each, build three sentences in your head: what's his/her name, where is he/she from, what does he/she do. Each time, notice whether the person is male or female, and make sure the ending ـهُ / ـهَا and the ة change with it.
It sounds trivial. But this is exactly where learners slip most often throughout A1 — not because they don't know the rule, but because English never forces them to think about it.

exercises.prompt: Form the nationality word. Write the male form, then the female form.

items: Where are you from? (to a woman)
What do you do? (to a man)
I'm a teacher and a translator.
Your Arabic is good. (to a woman)

exercises.prompt: Correct the wrong sentences. Rewrite them in full with vowel marks.
Answer these questions about yourself in full sentences.

answers: مِصْرِيّ، مِصْرِيَّة — إِنْدُونِيسِيّ، إِنْدُونِيسِيَّة — يَابَانِيّ، يَابَانِيَّة — سُورِيّ، سُورِيَّة — أَمْرِيكِيّ، أَمْرِيكِيَّة — مَغْرِبِيّ، مَغْرِبِيَّة
أَنَا مِنْ إِنْدُونِيسِيَا. — مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟ — هِيَ مِصْرِيَّةٌ. — مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ — أَنَا مُدَرِّسٌ وَمُتَرْجِمٌ. — لُغَتُكِ جَيِّدَةٌ.
لَيْلَى مَغْرِبِيَّةٌ. — أَنَا مِنْ إِنْدُونِيسِيَا (or أَنَا إِنْدُونِيسِيٌّ). — هِيَ مُدَرِّسَةٌ فِي الْجَامِعَةِ. — مَا اسْمُكَ؟ — أَنَا مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ.
Sample answers: اِسْمِي بُودِي. — أَنَا مِنْ إِنْدُونِيسِيَا. — أَنَا مُهَنْدِسٌ. — نَعَمْ، أَنَا طَالِبٌ. — لُغَتِي اَلْإِنْدُونِيسِيَّةُ.
